title: Angles: Measuring, Types and Angle Facts
seo_title: Angles – Primary 5 Mathematics Worksheets with Answers (NERDC)
standard_text: Measure and draw angles with a protractor; name acute, right, obtuse and reflex angles; find angles on a straight line, at a point and in a triangle. (summary of the NERDC Primary 5 Mathematics curriculum)
meta_desc: Free Primary 5 maths worksheets on angles: acute, right, obtuse and reflex angles, using a protractor, angles on a straight line, angles at a point and angles in a triangle. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Angles in a triangle add up to 180°.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Acute: less than 90°. Right: exactly 90°. Obtuse: between 90° and 180°. Reflex: between 180° and 360°.
  • Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. Angles at a point add up to 360°.
  • The three angles in a triangle add up to 180°.

Examples

Example

Two angles on a line: 115° and x

180 − 115

Answer: x = 65°

Example

Triangle with 50° and 70°

180 − 50 − 70

Answer: 60°

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Reading the wrong scale on the protractorStart from the 0 on the arm of the angle.
Using 360° for a straight lineA straight line is 180°.
Thinking a longer arm means a bigger angleThe size is the amount of turn.

faq.a: An angle bigger than 180° and smaller than 360°.

faq.q: How many right angles make a straight line?

items.q: What type of angle is marked?
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 35°.
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight line: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 125°.

A reflex angle is bigger than a straight line: between 180° and 360°. Look at the arc: it goes round the outside. This angle is 230°. (The angle on the other side is 130°, but the arc marks the big angle.)

items.q: What type of angle is marked?
items.e: A right angle is exactly 90°, a quarter turn. The small square shows it. This angle is 90°. Turning the angle does not change its size.

A reflex angle is bigger than a straight line: between 180° and 360°. Look at the arc: it goes round the outside. This angle is 320°. (The angle on the other side is 40°, but the arc marks the big angle.)
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight line: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 160°.

items.q: What type of angle is marked?
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle: less than 90°. This angle is 70°.

A reflex angle is bigger than a straight line: between 180° and 360°. Look at the arc: it goes round the outside. This angle is 200°. (The angle on the other side is 160°, but the arc marks the big angle.)
Two arms that make a straight line make an angle of 180°, half a turn. This angle is 180°.
An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight line: between 90° and 180°. This angle is 100°.

items.q: An angle measures 175°. What type of angle is it?
items.e: An obtuse angle is bigger than a right angle but smaller than a straight line. 175° is more than 90° but less than 180°.

items.q: An angle measures 185°. What type of angle is it?
items.e: A reflex angle is bigger than a straight line. 185° is more than 180° but less than 360°.

items.q: An angle measures 89°. What type of angle is it?
items.e: An acute angle is smaller than a right angle. 89° is less than 90° (only just!).

items.q: An angle measures 270°. What type of angle is it?
items.e: A reflex angle is bigger than a straight line. 270° is more than 180° but less than 360°.

items.q: Which of these angles is reflex?
items.e: A reflex angle is more than 180°. Only 210° is more than 180°. 175° is close to 180°, but it is still obtuse.

items.q: Which of these angles is obtuse?
items.e: An obtuse angle is between 90° and 180°. 135° is the only one. 225° is more than 180°, so it is reflex.

items.q: A reflex angle is …
items.e: Reflex angles are bigger than a half turn (180°) but smaller than a whole turn (360°).

items.q: Hadiza says an angle of 190° is obtuse because it is bigger than 90°. Is she right?
c: No, it is a right angle
items.e: Obtuse angles are bigger than 90° but smaller than 180°. 190° is more than 180°, so it is reflex.

items.q: Which list goes from the smallest angle to the largest?
items.e: Acute is less than 90°, a right angle is 90°, obtuse is between 90° and 180°, and reflex is more than 180°.

items.q: At which time is the smaller angle between the hands of a clock acute?
items.e: At 1 o’clock the hands are 1 hour space apart: 30°, which is acute. 3 o’clock is a right angle (90°), 4 o’clock is obtuse (120°) and 6 o’clock is a straight line (180°).

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 40. The outer scale says 140 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 40° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 65. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 60 and 70 is 65. The outer scale says 115 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 65° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 110. The outer scale says 70 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 110° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 155. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 150 and 160 is 155. The outer scale says 25 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 155° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 80. The outer scale says 100 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 80° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the right, so read the inner scale, which starts at 0 on the right. The other arm crosses it at 135. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 130 and 140 is 135. The outer scale says 45 there, but it starts from the other side. The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 135° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 30. (The inner scale says 150 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 30° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 55. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 50 and 60 is 55. (The inner scale says 125 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 55° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 120. (The inner scale says 60 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 120° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 145. The small marks go up in 5s, so the mark between 140 and 150 is 145. (The inner scale says 35 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 145° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 70. (The inner scale says 110 there.) The angle is smaller than a right angle, so 70° makes sense.

items.q: What is the size of the angle?
items.e: The bottom arm is on 0 on the left, so read the outer scale, which starts at 0 on the left. The other arm crosses it at 100. (The inner scale says 80 there.) The angle is bigger than a right angle, so 100° makes sense.

items.q: Neither arm is on 0. What is the size of the angle?
items.e: On the inner scale one arm is at 20 and the other is at 95. The angle is the difference: 95° − 20° = 75°.

items.q: Neither arm is on 0. What is the size of the angle?
items.e: On the inner scale one arm is at 40 and the other is at 150. The angle is the difference: 150° − 40° = 110°.

items.q: Where do you put the centre of the protractor when you measure an angle?
c: at the end of an arm
in the middle of an arm
items.e: The centre goes on the vertex, where the two arms meet. Then line up one arm with 0.

items.q: One arm of an angle is on 0 of the outer scale. Which scale should you read?
c: the scale with the bigger number
the scale with the smaller number
items.e: Read the scale that starts at 0 on your arm. Here that is the outer scale.

items.q: Kemi measures an angle that is clearly smaller than a right angle. The arm crosses the protractor at 35 and 145. What is the angle?
items.e: An angle smaller than a right angle is less than 90°, so it is 35°. 145 is on the other scale.

items.q: Simi wants to draw an angle of 65°. She puts her line on 0 of the inner scale. Where should she make a mark?
items.e: Use the scale that starts at 0 on your line: the inner scale. Count up to 65 (the small mark between 60 and 70), make a dot, then join it to the vertex. The small marks go up in 5s, so 5 marks after 60 would be 85. On the outer scale, 65 would give 115°.

items.q: To find a reflex angle, Nonso measures the angle on the other side. It is 130°. What is the reflex angle?
items.e: The two angles go all the way round the vertex, so they add up to 360°. 360° − 130° = 230°. (50° comes from using 180° instead of 360°.)

items.q: A protractor only goes to 180°. How can you draw a reflex angle of 250°?
c: Draw 110°, then mark the angle outside it
Draw 70°, then mark the angle outside it
items.e: 360° − 250° = 110°. Draw an angle of 110°. The angle round the outside is then 250°. (250° − 180° = 70° is a different angle.)
Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. 180° − 40° = 140°.
Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. 180° − 115° = 65°. (360° − 115° = 245° is for angles at a point.)
The line is tilted, but it is still straight: 180° − 48° = 132°.
Angles on a straight line add up to 180°. 180° − 73° = 107°.

items.q: The angles are on a straight line. Find ∠e.
items.e: The small square shows a right angle: 90°. 90° + 35° = 125°, and 180° − 125° = 55°.
First add the angles you know: 48° + 70° = 118°. Then subtract from 180°: 180° − 118° = 62°.
25° + 95° = 120°. Angles on a straight line add up to 180°, so 180° − 120° = 60°.

items.q: The angles are on a straight line. Find ∠h.
The two angles marked m are equal. Find ∠m.
items.e: 180° − 70° = 110°. The two equal angles share it: 110° ÷ 2 = 55°.
∠AOC and ∠BOC are on the straight line AOB, so they add up to 180°. ∠BOC = 180° − 128° = 52°.

items.q: Yusuf says ∠k = 50°, because it looks the same size as the 50° angle. Is he right?
items.e: Do not trust how an angle looks: work it out. 50° + 76° = 126°, and 180° − 126° = 54°.

items.q: The whole angle is a right angle. Find ∠n.
items.e: A right angle is 90°. 90° − 62° = 28°. (180° − 62° = 118° is for a straight line.)
The angles are on a straight line, so they add up to 180°, not 360°. 180° − 130° = 50°.

items.q: Angles on a straight line add up to …
items.e: A straight line makes a half turn: 180°. Two right angles make a straight line.

items.q: Two angles are on a straight line. One of them is 74°. Find the other angle.
Three equal angles together make a straight line. Find the size of each angle.
items.e: The three angles add up to 180°. 180° ÷ 3 = 60°. (120° comes from using 360°.)

items.q: Two angles are next to each other. One is 125° and the other is 65°. Can they make a straight line?
items.e: 125° + 65° = 190°. Angles on a straight line must add up to exactly 180°, so they cannot.

items.q: Two angles are on a straight line. One angle is 4 times as big as the other. Find the smaller angle.
items.e: The angles are 1 unit and 4 units: 5 units = 180°. 1 unit = 180° ÷ 5 = 36°. (The larger angle is 4 × 36° = 144°.)

items.q: Two angles are on a straight line. One is an acute angle of 38°. What is the other angle?
items.e: 180° − 38° = 142°. It is between 90° and 180°, so it is obtuse. (52° is 90° − 38°, which is for a right angle.)

items.q: A straight line is split into three angles. Two of them are 65° and 47°. Find the third angle.
items.e: 65° + 47° = 112°. 180° − 112° = 68°. (112° is the two angles added, not the unknown angle.)
Angles at a point add up to 360°. 110° + 135° = 245°, and 360° − 245° = 115°.
The small square is 90°. 90° + 125° + 60° = 275°, and 360° − 275° = 85°. (175° comes from forgetting the right angle.)
One angle is a reflex angle. 200° + 95° = 295°, and 360° − 295° = 65°.
Angles at a point add up to 360°. 360° − 130° = 230°. (50° comes from using 180°, and 490° from adding.)
Angles at a point add up to 360°. 360° ÷ 3 = 120°. (180° ÷ 3 = 60° is for a straight line.)
360° − 100° = 260°. The two equal angles share it: 260° ÷ 2 = 130°.
360° − 120° = 240°. ∠p is 1 unit and ∠q is 2 units: 3 units = 240°, so 1 unit = 80°. (120° comes from treating the two angles as equal.)
Add the angles you know, then subtract from 360°: 360° − 250° = 110°. 250° is the total of the two angles, not the unknown angle.

items.q: Two straight lines cross. Find ∠a.
items.e: ∠a is vertically opposite the 40° angle. Vertically opposite angles are equal, so ∠a = 40°.

items.q: Two straight lines cross. Find ∠b.
items.e: ∠b is vertically opposite the 65° angle. Vertically opposite angles are equal, so ∠b = 65°.

items.q: Two straight lines cross. Find ∠c.
items.e: ∠c is vertically opposite the 72° angle. Vertically opposite angles are equal, so ∠c = 72°.
∠d is vertically opposite the 145° angle. Vertically opposite angles are equal, so ∠d = 145°.
∠e is vertically opposite the 155° angle. Vertically opposite angles are equal, so ∠e = 155°.
∠f and 58° are next to each other on a straight line, so they add up to 180°. 180° − 58° = 122°. (They are not vertically opposite.)
∠g and 130° are next to each other on a straight line, so they add up to 180°. 180° − 130° = 50°. (They are not vertically opposite.)
∠h and 75° are next to each other on a straight line, so they add up to 180°. 180° − 75° = 105°. (They are not vertically opposite.)
∠m and 146° are next to each other on a straight line, so they add up to 180°. 180° − 146° = 34°. (They are not vertically opposite.)
∠p is on a straight line with 64°: 180° − 64° = 116°. ∠q is vertically opposite 64°, so it is 64°. ∠r is vertically opposite ∠p, so it is 116°.

items.q: The three angles of any triangle add up to
items.e: The angles of every triangle add up to 180°. (360° is the total for a four-sided figure such as a square.)

items.q: Find ∠x.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 50° + 60° = 110°, and 180° − 110° = 70°. Subtract both known angles, not just one.

items.q: Find ∠x.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 35° + 70° = 105°, and 180° − 105° = 75°. Subtract both known angles, not just one.

items.q: Find ∠x.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 25° + 115° = 140°, and 180° − 140° = 40°. Subtract both known angles, not just one.

items.q: Find ∠x.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 64° + 72° = 136°, and 180° − 136° = 44°. Subtract both known angles, not just one.

items.q: Find ∠x.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 45° + 105° = 150°, and 180° − 150° = 30°. Subtract both known angles, not just one.

items.q: Find ∠x.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 55° + 77° = 132°, and 180° − 132° = 48°. Subtract both known angles, not just one.

items.q: Find ∠PRQ.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 48° + 62° = 110°, and 180° − 110° = 70°.

items.q: Find ∠LKM.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 34° + 46° = 80°, and 180° − 80° = 100°.

items.q: Find ∠DEF.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 57° + 52° = 109°, and 180° − 109° = 71°.

items.q: In triangle PQR, ∠P = 47° and ∠Q = 68°. Find ∠R.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 47° + 68° = 115°, and 180° − 115° = 65°.

items.q: In triangle ABC, ∠A = 112° and ∠B = 29°. Find ∠C.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 112° + 29° = 141°, and 180° − 141° = 39°.

items.q: In triangle XYZ, ∠X = 38° and ∠Z = 85°. Find ∠Y.
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 38° + 85° = 123°, and 180° − 123° = 57°.

items.q: Two angles of a triangle are 73° and 54°. What is the third angle?
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 73° + 54° = 127°, and 180° − 127° = 53°.

items.q: Two angles of a triangle are 26° and 19°. What is the third angle?
items.e: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. 26° + 19° = 45°, and 180° − 45° = 135°.

items.q: Which set of angles can be the three angles of a triangle?
items.e: 50° + 60° + 70° = 180°, so these angles work. The others do not add up to 180°: 50°, 60°, 80° add up to 190°; 90°, 45°, 55° add up to 190°; 100°, 50°, 40° add up to 190°.

items.q: Usman draws a big triangle and a small triangle. He says the angles of the big triangle add up to more. Is he correct?
c: No, the small one has more
items.e: The angles of every triangle add up to 180°, big or small. A bigger triangle has longer sides, not bigger angles.

items.q: Blessing tears off the 3 corners of a paper triangle and puts them together, point to point. What do they make?
items.e: The 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180°, so the 3 corners fit together to make a straight line.

items.q: Can a triangle have angles of 95° and 85°?
items.e: 95° + 85° = 180°. That leaves 0° for the third angle, so these cannot be two angles of a triangle.

items.q: Which set of angles can be the three angles of a triangle?
items.e: 35° + 65° + 80° = 180°, so these angles work. The others do not add up to 180°: 35°, 65°, 90° add up to 190°; 60°, 60°, 70° add up to 190°; 120°, 30°, 40° add up to 190°.
